The mobile-manipulation region-goal method offers a concrete design principle: define a subgoal by the initiation set of the next controller. A navigation subgoal is valid when at least one inverse-kinematics solution exists for the manipulation phase. This removes the need for a perfect single point and makes the handoff robust to small pose errors.

The same principle applies beyond manipulation:

- a vehicle waypoint should admit a dynamically feasible continuation;
- a UAV waypoint should preserve sufficient energy to reach a landing or charging site;
- a multi-robot formation waypoint should preserve separation and communication;
- a human-aware navigation waypoint should maintain a recoverable clearance margin.

The evidence supports this as a demonstrated mechanism in mobile manipulation and as a transferable planning principle elsewhere. A direct sparse-reward, hard-constrained vehicle evaluation is not yet provided.

### 5.3 Long-horizon credit assignment

HER changes trajectory planning from “reach the final destination or receive no useful signal” to “learn local reachability between many achieved states.” This can produce a library of local transitions that later compose into a global route.

MRHER extends this idea by relaying increasingly difficult subtasks. GEAPS adds directional transition skills around achieved goals. SG-Safe combines HER with safe subgoal guidance. Together, these mechanisms suggest a three-level decomposition:

1. relabel achieved states as local goals;
2. learn or discover short feasible transitions between them;
3. select and compose those transitions toward the final objective.

This decomposition is especially useful when the final route is long but local motion is repetitive. It is less useful when the environment contains irreversible transitions, hidden hazards, or strong coupling between distant decisions. CSD’s own analysis notes that its symmetrized distance may be unsuitable for highly asymmetric environments with irreversible transitions.

TGL provides a complementary theoretical warning. Directly aligning a policy with expert-labeled long trajectories is NP-complete in the general case. Under bounded realizability or tree-structured MDP assumptions, it can compute optimal policies in polynomial time; under unknown dynamics, it uses UCB-style exploration and obtains sublinear regret [Trajectory Graph Learning](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/d3f39e51f5f634fb16cc3e658f8512b9-Abstract-Conference.html). For planning, the implication is that useful structure—bounded branching, graph-like routes, or reusable motion primitives—is necessary to avoid an intractable long-trajectory search.

### 5.4 Collision, dynamics, and instantaneous feasibility

Intrinsic exploration cannot by itself enforce collision avoidance. Trajectory planners should therefore assign different responsibilities to the exploratory policy and the safety mechanism.

A practical division is:

- the exploratory component proposes candidate waypoints, route branches, or informative actions;
- a learned or analytical model predicts short-horizon consequences;
- a reachability, barrier, or shield module rejects or modifies actions that leave the recoverable set;
- a backup policy preserves safety when no task-progressing action is verified.

Wang et al.’s automated-vehicle method embodies this design. RL proposes an action-induced trajectory, reachability predicts the occupancy of traffic participants, and the safety layer replaces unsafe intent with the closest safe trajectory before replanning [Wang et al. (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1109/tiv.2023.3344226). This is a direct mapping from RL exploration to trajectory generation and from reachability to safety verification.

Robust HJ-CBF and GP recovery shielding add model mismatch handling. HJ-CBF adapts its threshold using local slack; GP recovery estimates whether the state is recoverable and switches to a backup controller when necessary. DMPS further incorporates task value into recovery, reducing the frequency of interventions compared with a task-oblivious shield.

The main limitation is computational and informational. Reachability sets, GP uncertainty propagation, MPC, and action projection require models, state estimates, or conservative approximations. Under partial observability, a state that appears safe may not be safe for every underlying configuration consistent with the observation. SG-Safe avoids such explicit models but only offers expected-cost training safety, not a formal execution-time guarantee.

### 5.5 Dynamic obstacles and unknown environments

Dynamic obstacles create a distinction between a trajectory that is safe now and one that will remain safe after the environment changes.

DYNUS addresses dynamic unknown environments by maintaining exploratory, safe, and contingency trajectories. It samples safe backups from an exploratory trajectory, switches to the closest safe trajectory when the committed path becomes unsafe, and generates a contingency trajectory when no safe backup remains. Safe and contingency trajectories are generated in microseconds. Across dense forests, offices, caves, and dynamic environments, the study reports 100% success and travel times approximately 25% faster than state-of-the-art methods, with experiments on a quadrotor, wheeled robot, and quadruped in simulation and hardware [DYNUS](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.16734).

DYNUS is primarily a model-based planner rather than evidence that sparse-reward RL has solved dynamic-obstacle exploration. Its assumptions include non-adversarial obstacles, onboard detection, trackable dynamically feasible trajectories, and relatively consistent obstacle motion. A bug trap deeper than the local sensing range can prevent recovery.

SafeDrive uses a trajectory-conditioned sparse world model for end-to-end driving. Its Sparse World Network simulates critical dynamic agents and road entities, while its Fine-grained Reasoning Network evaluates pairwise collision risk and time-wise drivable-area compliance. On the open-loop NAVSIM dataset, it reports PDMS 91.6, EPDMS 87.5, and 61 collisions in 12,146 scenes, or 0.5%; on closed-loop Bench2Drive it reports a 66.8% driving score [SafeDrive](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2026/papers/Kim_SafeDrive_Fine-Grained_Safety_Reasoning_for_End-to-End_Driving_in_a_Sparse_CVPR_2026_paper.pdf).

SafeDrive demonstrates fine-grained trajectory evaluation rather than sparse-reward exploration. It is relevant because it evaluates which surrounding agent creates risk and at which time step, an ability that aggregate scene-level scores lack.

The CVaR barrier-function crowd-navigation method addresses stochastic moving obstacles with a Gaussian-mixture uncertainty model and probabilistic safety layer. Its guarantee is finite-horizon and sampled-data, and its simulation grants oracle uncertainty parameters. It therefore illustrates the type of risk-aware trajectory mechanism needed for dynamic obstacles while also showing why deployment assumptions must be reported explicitly.

### 5.6 Uncertainty and robustness

Trajectory planning should distinguish three forms of uncertainty:

1. **Epistemic uncertainty:** the planner lacks data about a new region, object, or dynamic regime.
2. **Aleatoric uncertainty:** the environment is intrinsically stochastic, such as wind or pedestrian motion.
3. **Model mismatch:** the learned or analytical dynamics differ from the real system.

Intrinsic information gain is most useful for epistemic uncertainty. Empowerment and risk penalties can prevent the agent from treating irreducible randomness as an attractive target. RAZER’s optimism–pessimism split provides a planning formulation for this distinction.

Model mismatch affects both exploration and safety. The model-based PPO-Lagrangian study shows how truncated model rollouts can underestimate cost. Lu et al.’s Turtlebot experiment deliberately creates a mismatch between the reachability model and actual angular-velocity limits. SHIELD learns hardware residuals and provides probabilistic safety under assumptions about their distribution. Adaptive Shielding infers hidden dynamics parameters online.

The implication for trajectory planning is that uncertainty should enter both waypoint selection and trajectory verification. A planner should not merely choose the shortest predicted path; it should consider the distribution of possible paths, the recoverability of deviations, and the confidence of the model in each segment.

### 5.7 Resource constraints: energy, fuel, time, and compute

Resource constraints change trajectory planning from “reach the goal safely” to “reach the goal while preserving the ability to finish.”

SEA-MAPPO treats battery depletion as a hard multi-robot safety constraint. It combines dense goal-distance reward, energy and load-balancing terms, predictive action masking, and safety shaping. In a seven-robot Robotarium navigation task, the study reports 95% goal completion after 0.49 million environment steps versus 9.36 million for MAPPO, 100% versus 81.5% goal completion at 10 million steps, and a 93.2% reduction in cumulative depletion. At convergence, SEA-MAPPO achieved \(0.809\pm0.026\) mean final battery and \(99.8\pm0.1\)% fleet readiness. On physical GTernal robots, it achieved 100% goal completion and zero depletion events across 70 robot-trials, with an energy-predictor \(R^2=0.89\) [SEA-MAPPO](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-6581/15/5/95).

This is strong evidence for predictive resource masking in trajectory execution, but it is not a direct sparse-reward intrinsic-exploration result. The task reward is dense negative goal distance, and collision avoidance is delegated to a lower-level CBF stack.

For UAVs, an adaptive nonlinear model-predictive-horizon planner uses DDPG or SAC to tune the parameters of a constrained NMPH optimizer. A global planner generates terminal points in unexplored regions of an incrementally built volumetric map; NMPH then plans a constrained trajectory to each terminal point [Adaptive NMPH](https://doi.org/10.3390/drones6110323). This demonstrates a useful division of labor between global exploration and local constrained optimization, but it does not isolate the contribution of sparse-reward exploration.

Energy-aware predictive MPC provides a non-RL comparison. A hybrid-zonotope planner couples vehicle motion and energy, using constrained zonotopes for state/input limits and hybrid zonotopes for nonconvex obstacle regions. In a fixed-wing UAS case, its structure-exploiting MIQP solved in 0.86 seconds versus 2.75 seconds for Gurobi with H-representation polytopes [Energy-Aware Predictive Motion Planning](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.03189v2). The result shows that efficient constraint handling may come from exploiting model structure rather than from RL.

A 2025 UAV–UGV routing study formulates fuel-depletion risk as a CMDP. The state includes positions, UAV fuel, and mission points; infeasible actions are masked; a Lagrangian multiplier penalizes failure probability above a threshold. In a 20 km × 20 km simulation, the UAV speed was 12 m/s, fuel capacity 150 kJ, and UGV speed 4.5 m/s. In a U45G15 comparison, Ra-DRL reported 260 minutes objective, 2.06 seconds solution time, and 0.01% risk, while a neural heuristic reported 531 minutes, 0.13 seconds, and 0.63% risk. The narrative and table disagree about one threshold label—\(\delta=0.5\) or \(\delta=0.05\)—so the risk comparison requires qualification [Mondal et al. (2025)](https://aliothy.github.io/luca_russo_portfolio/files/papers/ICRA_2025.pdf).

A 2026 low-altitude UAV study combines SAC with LLM reasoning in a partially observable model containing obstacle, regulation, and energy constraints. It reports a 99.50% data-collection rate, nearly 100% successful landing, almost-zero collision and regulation-violation rates, and a 76.95% energy-consumption rate [Safe and Economical UAV Trajectory Planning](https://doi.org/10.1109/tmc.2026.3668209). These are abstract-level results, and the source does not provide a common denominator or detailed comparison of constraint violations.

Time and computation are also resources. SG-Safe removes the subgoal policy at inference, avoiding online hierarchical planning. On POLAMP, it reports zero online planning time and approximately 10× faster inference than Lyapunov-RRT. DMPS improves task progress but incurs planning overhead that grows with horizon. DYNUS generates safe backups in microseconds. A trajectory-planning system should therefore report planning latency alongside success and safety.

### 5.8 Informative trajectory planning

Not all exploration planning is about reaching a fixed goal. Li et al. formulate informative trajectory planning for an autonomous vehicle exploring an unknown spatiotemporal field. The objective is minimum-time travel subject to a cumulative information constraint based on an observability measure. Field approximations create dense rewards, and simulations report shorter exploration time than a coverage planner once sufficient cumulative information is obtained [Li et al. (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1109/tnnls.2023.3300926).

This is evidence that domain-informed reward densification can improve planning efficiency, but it is not evidence that intrinsic curiosity, HER, or skill discovery solves sparse-reward planning. The information constraint is cumulative, and the supplied result does not report collision or instantaneous feasibility metrics.

The planning implication is that information gain should be treated as a task objective or constraint with physical meaning. A generic novelty bonus can be replaced or complemented by expected reduction in map uncertainty, observability, target detectability, or model uncertainty. The same system still needs collision and dynamics safety mechanisms.

### 5.9 Data requirements and sim-to-real deployment

Real-world evidence is strongest when it reports both training data and deployment failures.

- LaNE reports under-one-hour RL training on a Franka Panda using a few demonstrations.
- DemoStart reports zero-shot transfer from simulation and 100 times fewer demonstrations than learning-from-demonstration policies.
- Lu et al. demonstrate safe Turtlebot learning under deliberate model mismatch with minimal human intervention.
- SHIELD demonstrates probabilistic obstacle avoidance on a Unitree G1 using hardware residual data.
- SEA-MAPPO reports zero depletion across 70 physical robot-trials without fine-tuning.
- CCE reports an 18% higher success rate, 20–38% shorter paths, and 9.32% lower elevation costs under a fixed sample budget, including deployment on a Clearpath Husky [CCE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.06192).

Other studies require more cautious interpretation. Steinecker et al. synchronize a real vehicle with a virtual vehicle, predict 40 trajectory points at 0.1 s resolution over a 4-second horizon, and test on a 1.9 km track. But the authors explicitly state that they do not analyze the performance of the trajectory-generating or RL agents because that performance is independent of their sim-to-real method [Steinecker et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.07155). The hardware demonstration therefore validates synchronization, not the learned planner’s task performance.

Similarly, a quadrotor local planner reports simulation-to-real success improvements over DRL and artificial-potential-field baselines, including a 50% higher real-time success rate than its DRL baseline. But its reward contains explicit dense progress and safety-boundary penalties, and the authors note that neural methods do not provide the mathematical stability guarantees of control-theoretic approaches [Ugurlu, Pham, and Kayacan (2022)](https://doi.org/10.3390/robotics11050109).

The practical conclusion is that sim-to-real evidence must identify what transferred: the policy, the dynamics model, the safety layer, the energy predictor, or only the controller interface. A real vehicle on a track is not by itself evidence that sparse-reward policy exploration is safe under dynamic obstacles.

## 6. Transferable insights, limitations, and open problems

### 6.1 What is directly demonstrated

The literature supports several conclusions with reasonably strong evidence.

First, hindsight and model-based replay can materially improve sample efficiency in multi-goal sparse-reward tasks. HER has clear toy and Fetch evidence; I-HER reports 4–30× less real data on four Fetch tasks; MRHER reports 13.79% and 14.29% improvements over RHER on two Fetch benchmarks.

Second, structured goal exploration is more effective than generic state novelty when the goal representation matters. GEAPS improves PointMaze and AntMaze exploration; its comparison against LEXA shows that state novelty does not necessarily translate into goal coverage. CSD demonstrates that controllability-aware diversity can discover object manipulation that MI and Euclidean diversity miss.

Third, safe exploration benefits from mechanisms that preserve task progress. DMPS reduces shield interventions while increasing return; robust HJ-CBF reduces violations under model mismatch; proactive action replacement reduces real-robot intervention rates; SG-Safe uses subgoals and HER to avoid the stationary policies produced by overly conservative Lagrangian learning.

Fourth, resource constraints can be handled as safety constraints rather than merely reward penalties. SEA-MAPPO’s predictive battery masking and physical deployment results are a concrete example. The BESS active-exploration study similarly shows how a conservative engineering solution can guide RL without necessarily becoming the final policy.

Fifth, hard safety claims are conditional. Reachability, CBF, GP, and conformal methods require models, invariant sets, disturbance assumptions, or uncertainty calibration. Lagrangian methods require accurate cost estimates and do not generally prevent training violations. A final-policy zero-violation result is not the same as zero violations throughout training.

### 6.2 Demonstrated combinations versus transfer hypotheses

The following combinations have direct evidence:

- **HER + hierarchical safe RL:** SG-Safe combines HER, subgoal guidance, and a Lagrangian safety objective in Safety Gym and POLAMP.
- **Intrinsic skill discovery + safety critics:** SASD combines mutual-information skill discovery and a safety critic in simulated manipulation.
- **Constrained intrinsic objectives:** CIM constrains representation learning and adaptively weights intrinsic objectives in MuJoCo.
- **Resource-aware action masking + multi-agent RL:** SEA-MAPPO combines predictive masking, energy rewards, and lower-level collision safety, including hardware deployment.
- **Model-based exploration + trajectory optimization:** CEE-US combines epistemic disagreement and iCEM planning, but without physical safety constraints.
- **Risk-aware RL + reachability verification:** VIA combines CVaR training and post-training per-timestep verification, but not a multi-step trajectory guarantee.

The following are promising but incompletely validated transfer hypotheses:

- GEAPS or CSD skills combined with an HJ-CBF or GP recovery shield;
- novelty or empowerment used to select only candidate waypoints inside a reachable safe set;
- HER with CVaR or chance-constrained cost critics on dynamic-obstacle planning;
- world-model disagreement constrained by a safe backup planner;
- demonstration-guided exploration with conformal safety bounds;
- resource-aware novelty that values information only when the remaining battery, fuel, or time budget permits recovery;
- risk-aware skill graphs whose edges are annotated with success distributions, intervention frequency, and resource consumption.

No supplied study validates all of these combinations on a common trajectory-planning benchmark with sparse terminal feedback, hard instantaneous constraints, dynamic obstacles, model mismatch, and sim-to-real evaluation.

### 6.3 Open problem 1: a joint exploration-and-safety benchmark

The most immediate gap is evaluation. Sparse-reward papers usually report success, return, coverage, or sample use. Safe-RL papers report cost, collision, intervention, or risk. Trajectory-planning papers add path length, time, clearance, energy, and computation. These metrics are rarely measured together.

A useful benchmark should include:

- a terminal or very sparse task reward;
- explicit geometric and kinodynamic constraints;
- static and dynamic obstacles;
- partial observability;
- controllable and irreducible uncertainty;
- resource budgets;
- a simulator and a hardware or high-fidelity deployment track;
- common training and inference budgets.

The benchmark should report discovery time, goal coverage, task success, return, cumulative cost, instantaneous violation frequency, maximum consecutive unsafe steps, violation severity, interventions, path quality, resource use, training safety, final-policy safety, and cross-task generalization.

Safety Gymnasium, Dubins reach-avoid, Turtlebot, POLAMP, mobile manipulation, and multi-robot battery tasks provide useful components, but none alone spans the complete requirement.

### 6.4 Open problem 2: safe directed goal discovery

Sparse-reward methods need to propose new goals; safety methods need to reject unsafe behavior. The difficult question is how to make the goal-selection process itself safety-aware.

A possible design is to score a candidate goal \(g\) by a combination of:

- progress toward the final task;
- novelty or information gain;
- probability of reaching \(g\);
- probability of remaining in a recoverable set;
- expected resource consumption;
- tail risk under model uncertainty.

The safety score should not merely penalize the trajectory after execution. It should determine whether the goal is eligible for exploration. A candidate waypoint near an obstacle may be informative, but it should be selected only if a safe approach and recovery route exist.

This is a hypothesis grounded in the separate evidence from GEAPS, CSD, ORAC, and reachability shielding. It has not been validated as a unified method.

### 6.5 Open problem 3: hard instantaneous constraints with sparse feedback

HER can make failed episodes useful, but a failed episode that contains a collision may be unacceptable. A hard shield can prevent the collision, but it may also prevent the transition needed to reach the goal. The resulting replay buffer may contain only safe but uninformative behavior.

A promising solution is to relabel only safe achieved states and to train a goal-conditioned policy over a dynamically feasible safe-transition graph. The graph could use:

- HER for local goal labels;
- skill discovery for reusable edges;
- reachability or barrier verification for edge admissibility;
- uncertainty-aware cost distributions for edge reliability;
- a recovery action for every selected edge.

The challenge is preserving exploration near the boundary without crossing it. The source literature demonstrates each ingredient separately, but not the full graph construction under hard constraints.

### 6.6 Open problem 4: model mismatch and partial observability

Most formal safety guarantees assume a known or bounded model. Most sparse-reward methods assume that the state or goal representation is adequate. Real trajectory planning violates both assumptions.

Under partial observation, the same lidar scan can correspond to multiple hidden obstacle configurations. Under model mismatch, a policy may select a trajectory that is safe in simulation but not on hardware. The agent therefore needs a belief-aware or uncertainty-aware safety representation.

Several recent mechanisms point toward a solution:

- adaptive hidden-parameter inference;
- conformal prediction for risk bounds;
- GP residual models;
- robust HJ reachability;
- stochastic CBFs;
- hardware residual learning;
- noise augmentation and domain randomization.

The open issue is computational and statistical: uncertainty estimates must be calibrated in the regions the exploratory policy visits, including rare states near obstacles and dynamic interactions. A model that is accurate on ordinary trajectories can still be unsafe exactly where a novelty policy wants to go.

### 6.7 Open problem 5: resource-aware exploration and planning

Energy, fuel, time, and compute budgets should not be treated as secondary reward terms when exhaustion causes mission failure. SEA-MAPPO shows the value of predictive action masking for battery depletion. The UAV–UGV, BESS, adaptive NMPH, and hybrid-zonotope studies show that resource-aware planning can materially change the feasible route set.

The unresolved problem is how to allocate resources to exploration itself. Information-gathering trajectories may be longer, slower, or more energy-intensive than direct routes. A planner should decide when additional information is worth its cost and whether the remaining budget permits recovery.

A useful formulation would treat information gain as a reward or constraint, collision and dynamics as instantaneous hard constraints, and energy or fuel as a remaining-budget state. The policy would then select exploration actions only if the resulting belief state retains a feasible route to completion. Current studies address these components separately.

### 6.8 Open problem 6: scalable multi-agent safe exploration

Multi-robot trajectory planning adds coupled constraints. One robot’s action changes another robot’s collision risk, energy allocation, communication range, or access to a shared waypoint.

SEA-MAPPO demonstrates centralized training with decentralized execution for seven robots and evaluates fleet sizes of four, seven, and fourteen. Safe multi-agent literature also includes MACPO and decentralized constrained policy optimization. But sparse-reward goal discovery and hard multi-agent safety are rarely studied together.

The difficult cases include:

- dynamic fleets in which agents enter or leave;
- heterogeneous battery capacities and dynamics;
- limited communication;
- shared narrow corridors;
- unknown or adversarial behavior by other agents;
- decentralized guarantees for global separation constraints.

A subgoal policy that proposes independently safe waypoints may still create a joint collision. A global shield may be computationally prohibitive. The missing theory concerns how to decompose joint reachability and resource constraints without losing safety.

### 6.9 Open problem 7: training safety versus final-policy safety

The literature often reports one of three different claims:

1. the final policy satisfies an expected cost limit;
2. the training process experiences fewer violations;
3. every executed action is verified safe under specified assumptions.

These are not interchangeable. Lagrangian methods usually target the first and may improve the second. Action masking and shielding target the third, but only relative to their models or safety sets. SSAC reports zero violations for converged policies; SEA-MAPPO reports zero depletion in hardware trials; neither result alone proves universal safety throughout all training or deployment conditions.

Future evaluations should plot safety over training and report:

- number and severity of violations before convergence;
- longest consecutive unsafe sequence;
- intervention rate and intervention type;
- final-policy safety under nominal and shifted conditions;
- safety under sensor and actuator noise;
- proportion of episodes in which the shield has no feasible action;
- degradation when the safety model is deliberately misspecified.

### 6.10 Practical design principles for trajectory-planning researchers

The evidence supports several cautious design principles.

First, make exploration task-relevant. Use goal, object, map, observability, or controllability representations rather than assuming generic novelty is useful.

Second, separate discovery from execution safety. Let an intrinsic or hierarchical policy propose candidate regions, but verify collision, dynamics, and resource feasibility before execution.

Third, treat subgoals as regions or initiation sets when exact points create infeasible handoffs. A waypoint is useful only if the next controller can start from it.

Fourth, use replay to create local learning signals, but do not assume relabeling can replace missing first-contact or first-entry behavior. Demonstrations, safe priors, or model-based planning may still be necessary.

Fifth, distinguish uncertainty that exploration can reduce from uncertainty that should be avoided. Combining information gain with empowerment or risk estimates is more defensible than rewarding all prediction error.

Sixth, evaluate safety during training, not only after convergence. A method that reaches a safe final policy through many collisions is unsuitable for physical online learning.

Seventh, report resource and computation costs. A method that improves success while using ten times the planning latency or an unrealistic energy model may not improve the deployed planner.

## Closing judgment

Recent reinforcement learning has moved exploration from random action noise toward structured discovery and from passive cost penalties toward proactive feasibility management. Sparse-reward research has become better at finding goals, relabeling failure, composing skills, using demonstrations, and planning with learned models. Constraint-aware research has become better at handling cumulative costs, tail risk, model uncertainty, recovery, reachability, and resource depletion.

For trajectory planning, neither line is sufficient on its own. Efficient discovery without safety can produce irrelevant or hazardous trajectories; safety without directed discovery can produce conservative policies that never reach distant goals. The strongest research direction is a task-directed hierarchy or world model coupled to uncertainty-aware feasibility checks, recoverable subgoals, and explicit reporting of both exploration progress and training-time safety. The central scientific challenge is no longer simply to make an agent explore more or collide less, but to make it discover useful trajectories while preserving a verified path to remain feasible.
